newsitem.title: INDIA: New India satellite policy a small step forward.
newsitem.headline: New India satellite policy a small step forward.

text.p: India's decision to end a state monopoly on satellites is only a small step towards freeing telecommunications and broadcasting from government control, industry analysts said on Sunday.

"It is long overdue, but this permission to allow ownership of satellites should have been part of a larger package that talks about uplinking and telecom and the costs involved," said Mahesh Uppal, an independent telecommunications analyst.
India said last week it would allow private firms to use transponders on state satellites and permit private users to establish commercial communications satellites.
Firms would be allowed to use either Indian or foreign satellites while operating out of India, but the government said Indian satellites would be given preferential treatment.
Until now, India barred private firms from owning satellites and from using transponders on the state-run Indian National Satellite System (INSAT).

Uppal said the benefits of liberalising satellites would appear only after parliament passed a bill allowing broadcasters to air signals from India, and considered allowing private telephone firms to establish long-distance networks.

"India is one of the world leaders in space technology. For a country like this to have independent television producers literally carting their cassettes to Hong Kong and obscure parts of the world is absurd," Uppal told Reuters.
Private firms are not allowed to beam signals out of India. Satellite broadcasters, led by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp-owned Star TV, currently broadcast to India from Hong Kong and other centres.

U.R. Rao, a former chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) which owns INSAT, said the government must ease controls on broadcasting to utilise excess satellite capacity. India is one of half a dozen countries with an independent space programme, headed by ISRO.
"It is a step in the right direction but what is required is more liberalisation," Rao, also a member of the Indian Space Commission, told Reuters in the southern city of Bangalore.
"We should go further to catch up with the global satellite market," Rao said. "The restrictions on direct-to-home services should go and uplinking should be provided to private agencies."
Uppal said the government must now examine laws on telecommunications as well. "Several other regulatory decisions still have to come," he said.

"Its real impact will be felt when long-distance telephony is opened to private operators. Satellites are effective when the size of a country is an issue, and satellite communications in a country like India are a phenomenal opportunity."
India began privatising basic telephone services in 1995, but inter-state and international calls must still be routed through the government Department of Telecommunications network.
Uppal said the government would need to quickly spell out commercial details so that firms could calculate costs.
"What you will do with the capacity and how you will get a return on it still has to be worked out," he said. "If ISRO ends up charging huge fees, then this permission is as good as not there."

"ISRO will probably be forced to respond to market forces because there is no obligation to buy from them, but because people book satellite capacity years in advance, there might be dependence on ISRO in the short run," Uppal added.
